column1: Follow-up on story 1. What was the hardest part?
column2: Honestly, it was inside the company. The natural reaction was to oppose it. I had to show our leaders that the goal had real momentum and that a flat no would cost us the room. Once they saw that, we could put our energy into shaping it instead of fighting it.

column1: Follow-up on story 1. What ended up in CRGA, and do you count that as a win?
column2: What passed was a pilot approach, with financing available through the Illinois Finance Authority. Yes, I count it as a win. What passed is something a utility can implement and customers can afford, and it reflects the pilot-first approach we argued for.

column1: Follow-up on story 1. Who were the key decision makers?
column2: The sponsor, the House Energy and Environment Committee, leadership, the progressive caucus, legislators in our territory and the environmental organizations. Then I matched each one with the most credible messenger, whether that was one of our experts, an executive, a contract lobbyist or the industry association.

column1: Follow-up on story 1. How did you measure success?
column2: Four things. Problem provisions did not move before they were ready. Our concerns became part of the real policy conversation. Key relationships held up. And the issue moved toward something that could be implemented. Sometimes success is changing the direction so everyone ends up with better choices.

column1: Follow-up on story 2. What would you do if a legislator asked ComEd for something like that?
column2: Exactly the same thing. Be respectful, point them to the process, and tell my leadership and compliance that day. I would also make sure the whole team is trained so any one of us would give the same answer.

column1: Follow-up on story 2. How do you keep lobbyists and consultants in line with compliance?
column2: Everyone works from the same rules. We follow the state ethics rules and report out, a third-party auditor follows up twice a year, legal reinforces it, and our company president made compliance non-negotiable. I would hold contract lobbyists to the same standard and I would check, not assume.

column1: Follow-up on story 2. Was there a cost to saying no?
column2: There is always some risk when you tell a powerful person no. I managed it by keeping leadership informed and keeping my tone respectful. The cost of bending the rules would have been far higher.

column1: Phone screen. Walk me through your background.
column2:
Decision, eighteen years, roots, three things.
Sure. I’m a Senior Government Relations Representative at Ameren Illinois, and I’ve been in Government Relations for eighteen years. The short version is that I turn policy fights into decisions the company can stand behind, and then I win support for them in Springfield. Today I’m my department’s lead on data center, battery storage and decarbonization bills, and I work closely with legal, regulatory, operations and our executives to get to one company position. Before Government Relations, I ran a health and welfare plan with a staff of seven and a board of trustees, and I spent five years in Ameren’s HR group, including two mergers and the company’s first shared services model. So I bring Springfield, the business behind the bill and real people leadership, and I’d love to bring that to ComEd.

column1: Phone screen. What interests you about this role?
column2:
Lead, same agenda, short list.
Three things. First, it’s a leadership role, leading the team and the company’s position on every state issue, and that’s the step I’m ready for. Second, ComEd’s agenda is the one I already work on, data centers, affordability, CRGA and grid planning. And third, ComEd has been on my short list for years, so when this opened, it felt like the right time.

column1: Phone screen. Why are you looking to leave Ameren?
column2:
Not running. Few seats. Ready to lead.
I’m not running from anything. I’ve had a great run at Ameren and a real seat at the table with senior leaders. Government Relations is a small function, and director roles don’t open often. I’m ready to lead with the title, and I’d rather do that at a company I’ve respected for a long time.

column1: Phone screen. What do you know about ComEd?
column2:
4 million, reliability, four big issues.
ComEd serves more than four million customers, about 70 percent of the state, and it’s the largest part of Exelon. Operationally it’s strong. It led its peers in reliability last year. The big issues right now are affordability with PJM capacity costs, data center growth and who pays for it, the second grid plan in front of the ICC, and implementing CRGA. Those are the same issues I work on every day from the Ameren side.

column2:

[Name] on the Government and Legislative Affairs team reached out and encouraged me to apply. I’ve followed ComEd for a long time, so I was glad to.

column1: Phone screen. The role calls for at least 12 years in the legislative arena. Tell me about yours.
column2:
Eighteen years, three big laws, a full bill portfolio.
I have eighteen years in Illinois government relations, working the General Assembly, the executive branch and the ICC. I’ve worked the major energy laws of that period, EIMA, CEJA and CRGA, and each session I manage a portfolio of bills from tracking, to expert review, to a company position, to advocacy.

column1: Phone screen. The posting asks for five years of supervisory experience. Tell me about that.
column2:
Seven, seven, five, plus the hard kind.
Yes. I ran Southwest Benefit Program for seven years with a staff of seven, plus our outside counsel and accountants, and I reported to a board of trustees. At Ameren I spent five years in HR advising managers on discipline, terminations, succession and labor relations, and supporting two merger integrations. And in Government Relations I train new team members on our processes and ethics, guide contract lobbyists and lead cross-functional teams on my issues. I’m ready to have a GR team on my own org chart.

column1: Phone screen. How would you describe your leadership style?
column2:
Clear, collaborative, no surprises.
Clear and collaborative. I set the goal and the deadline up front, bring the right people in early and let the experts own their piece. When the clock is running in session, I get more directive. And I don’t surprise my leaders. They hear from me first, good news or bad, with a recommendation attached.

column1: Phone screen. What is your experience working with senior executives?
column2:
Changed, means, decide.
A big part of my job is turning what’s happening in Springfield into something executives can act on. I do status reports, strategy calls and end-of-session reports, and in HR I worked with senior leaders on two mergers, the first shared services model, and executive pay and performance modeling. I keep it short. What changed, what it means and what we need to decide.

column1: Phone screen. Tell me about a recent accomplishment.
column2:
Thermal networks, tabled, then CRGA.
Thermal energy networks. In 2025 a decarbonization bill came in that we couldn’t live with as written. I set our internal strategy, we moved from opposing it to offering a pilot path, the bill was tabled, and a workable version became law in CRGA. I’d be glad to walk the panel through it.

column1: Phone screen. How do you approach ethics and compliance in lobbying?
column2:
Same rules, report up, audited.
Same rules for everyone, every time. I follow the state ethics rules and report out, a third-party auditor reviews our work twice a year, and our legal team reinforces it. I’ve been tested on that, when someone with influence pushed for something we couldn’t do, and I’m glad to share that example with the panel.

column1: Phone screen. Are you open to relocating to the Chicago area? The role is hybrid.
column2:
Yes, ready to move.
Yes. I’m ready to relocate to the Chicago area, and the hybrid schedule works well for me.

column1: Phone screen. The role involves frequent Springfield travel and long hours during storms. Any concerns?
column2:
None. Already doing both.
None at all. I’m in Springfield throughout session now, and I already work with our storm response team, including keeping legislators updated during outages. At this stage of life my schedule is my own.

column1: Phone screen. What are your salary expectations?
column2:
Upper half of the posted range, flexible on the package.
I saw the posted range of $164,800 to $226,600, plus the annual bonus and the long-term incentive. With eighteen years in Illinois government relations and the scope of this role, I’d expect to land in the upper half of that range, around [your target, for example $205,000 to $215,000]. I’m flexible on how the total package comes together. The role itself is what matters most to me.

column1: Phone screen. When could you start?
column2:
Professional transition, flexible date.
I’d give Ameren two to four weeks for a professional transition, and I’m flexible on the exact date.

column1: Phone screen. Are you interviewing anywhere else?
column2:
Selective. ComEd is the focus.
I’m being selective. ComEd is my focus right now.

column1: Phone screen. Do you have a non-compete or confidentiality obligations?
column2:
No non-compete. Confidential stays confidential.
I don’t have a non-compete. I do take confidentiality seriously. I won’t bring anything confidential from Ameren, and I’d expect ComEd to hold me to that.

column1: Phone screen. Are you a registered lobbyist in Illinois?
column2:
Registered, current.
Yes, I’m registered with the Illinois Secretary of State and my filings are current.

column1: Phone screen. What are your greatest strengths?
column2:
Inside alignment, plain language, long relationships.
Three come to mind. Getting a whole company to one position, legal, regulatory, operations and executives. Translating complicated policy into plain language for legislators and leaders. And relationships across the aisle that I’ve built and kept over eighteen years.

column1: Phone screen. What is a weakness you are working on?
column2:
Headline first.
I tend to give too much detail, because in my world leaving something out can hurt you. I’ve learned to lead with the answer and the decision we need, and keep the detail ready for whoever wants it.

column1: Phone screen. Where do you see yourself in five years?
column2:
A trusted team, people promoted.
Leading a team at ComEd that executives trust and legislators rely on, and having developed a few people who are ready for the next step themselves.

column1: Phone screen. Why should we move you forward?
column2:
The boxes, plus the extras.
I check the boxes the posting asks for, and I bring more. Eighteen years in Springfield, a business and HR background most lobbyists don’t have, real experience leading people and a track record of doing this work the right way. I’d welcome the chance to show the panel.

column1: Resume. Walk me through your resume.
column2:
Fund, HR, GR, Today.
I started as Program Director of a Taft-Hartley health benefit program covering about 25,000 union members in five states. I ran a staff of seven, managed our lawyers, accountants and administrators, and worked for a board of trustees. In 2003 I joined Ameren in benefits, then became a Senior HR Consultant, where I worked on efficiency and restructuring initiatives alongside firms like Accenture and IBM, two mergers and the company’s first shared services model. In 2008 I moved into Government Relations at Ameren Illinois. Today I lead our department’s work on data centers, battery storage and decarbonization, manage about 60 bills a session and lead the legislative workstream of Operation Resilient Grid.

column1: Resume. You have held the same title since 2008. Why?
column2:
Small function, family first, scope grew.
Two honest reasons. Earlier in my career I chose roles that fit what my family needed, and Government Relations is a small function where leadership seats rarely open. What grew was my scope. I went from carrying assigned bills to leading the department’s work on our biggest current issues, leading the legislative workstream on a major reliability initiative and briefing the president and officers directly.

column1: Resume. Your MBA is in health service management. How does that apply here?
column2:
Regulated, cost versus access, strategy.
More than you might think. Healthcare and utilities are both heavily regulated, and the core tension in both is cost versus access. Here it is affordability versus reliability. The Executive MBA gave me the finance, strategy and leadership tools, and I use them every time I weigh whether customers are paying a fair cost for something that lasts, without putting the business at unnecessary risk.

column1: Resume. What does leading the department’s work on data centers, storage and decarbonization look like day to day?
column2:
Point person, one team, one position.
I am Government Relations’ point person on those issues. I guide a cross-functional team of business leaders and experts from the internal position, through communications, to advocacy. On data centers I coordinate with Economic Development and our Clean Energy Transition team, prepare bill analyses for House and Senate hearings and keep a data center legislation knowledge center so the whole team stays current as bills move.

column1: Resume. How do you manage 60 bills a session?
column2:
Track, route, decide, brief.
With a system. Every assigned bill goes on a weekly tracker. Each one is routed to the right experts, I work with the responsible executive to reach a position before committee, and leadership gets intelligence briefings, written analyses and risk assessments as bills move. The goal is that nothing important reaches a committee without a company position behind it.

column1: Resume. Tell us about the SME routing tool.
column2:
109 topics, 25 sections, right expert fast.
It is a tool I built that matches any bill or issue to the right leader, department or team. It covers about 109 topics across 25 sections of an electric and gas utility. Before it, routing depended on who you happened to know. Now a bill reaches the right experts quickly, and we can settle positions before committee action. It grew out of a lesson I learned early, that watching a bill is not the same as managing it.

column1: Resume. How do you keep leadership informed?
column2:
Weekly, strategic, end of session, prepped.
Several ways, depending on what they need. Weekly newsletters and status reports, strategic calls when something is moving, end-of-session reports on activity, strategy and results, and briefings that prepare executives before they meet with policymakers. I keep each one short. What changed, what it means and what we need to decide.

column1: Resume. You work with a Deputy Governor. What does that relationship look like?
column2:
Raise ours, answer theirs, straight both ways.
It is a working relationship on energy policy. I raise the company’s concerns with the administration, and I respond when they bring issues or requests to us. It works because we are useful to each other and straight with each other.

column1: Resume. Your resume says you support the PAC process. What does that mean?
column2:
Working knowledge, objective process, inside the rules.
I want to be clear that I do not run Ameren’s PAC. I know its bylaws, contribution strategy and disclosure requirements well, and I coordinate three or four political fundraising events a year, more than 30 since 2017, all inside the state ethics and campaign finance rules. My view is that contributions follow an objective, documented process tied to policy, never a favor and never a grudge.

column1: Resume. How do you keep up with national trends?
column2:
EEI, AGA, EIA, what is coming to Illinois.
Through EEI and the American Gas Association, and by following Energy Information Administration data. I watch federal energy policy, MISO and PJM capacity changes and what other states are doing, because a lot of what lands in Springfield shows up somewhere else first. Then I translate that into what it could mean for our legislative strategy.

column1: Resume. What exactly was your role on EIMA, FEJA, CEJA and CRGA?
column2:
Support, support, connect, sustain.
I want to be precise, because these were big team efforts. On EIMA in 2011, I did the district work, including an educational tour with legislators and local leaders, and I received the President’s Performance Leadership Award. On FEJA in 2016, I supported passage, including the provisions that preserved the Clinton and Quad Cities nuclear plants and secured infrastructure provisions for us. On CEJA, I connected our internal teams to the legislative effort and kept communication moving. And on CRGA, I maintained key legislative relationships through a multi-year negotiation, and my two assigned issues, data access and thermal networks, were folded into the final law.

column1: Resume. Your cover letter mentions data access and thermal energy networks. What happened?
column2:
Already in place, technology limits. Measured until a pilot.
Both came back session after session, and both were assigned to me. I set the internal strategy and kept our team behind one position. On data access, we showed legislators that many of the provisions were already in place and that others ran into real technology limits, and the data retention requirement came down from fifteen years to five. On thermal networks, the original language did not balance what customers would pay against what they would get, so we held to a measured approach until a workable pilot came together. Both ended up in CRGA.

column1: Resume. Tell us about Operation Resilient Grid.
column2:
Five plants, 2,092 MW, $45 million, make it local.
It is a multi-track strategy to keep 2,092 MW of natural gas peaking capacity in central and southern Illinois from retiring under CEJA, at a time when data centers are pushing demand up. I lead the legislative workstream. That includes weekly cross-functional coordination, executive briefings, a legislator engagement matrix and coalition trackers for the 2026 to 2027 decision window. To make it local for downstate members, I built a fiscal impact case showing more than $45 million in cumulative property taxes paid to local governments and school districts. The point is that the clean energy transition still needs enough capacity for peak days.

column1: Resume. Why would Operation Resilient Grid matter to ComEd?
column2:
Same question in PJM.
Because PJM faces the same question. With load growing, is there enough capacity for peak days while older plants retire? The approach transfers. Build the reliability case, make it local for legislators and bring a coalition that includes labor and local governments.

column1: Resume. Tell us about your HR work alongside Accenture and IBM.
column2:
Efficiency with people in mind.
In my HR years Ameren went through a lot of change. I worked alongside Accenture and IBM on cost-saving and efficiency initiatives, helped introduce new operating structures and reduce duplication, and guided realignment from recruiting and onboarding to redeployment and separation. I also did compensation mapping and job analysis, worked on two mergers and the first shared services model, and built executive pay and performance models. The lesson was that efficiency only sticks when people understand why and are treated fairly along the way.

column1: Resume. At Southwest Benefit Program you managed lawyers, accountants and vendors. How did you hold them accountable?
column2:
Quality, compliance, cost, and the board.
I held every outside firm to the same standard. Clear expectations on service quality, compliance and cost, and regular reviews against them. I negotiated contracts with hospitals, pharmacy suppliers, therapy providers and equipment vendors, managed the budgets and audits, and prepared the board’s materials and recommendations. Working with our attorney, I also helped move the plan out from under heavy Department of Labor oversight. That is the same discipline I would bring to managing contract lobbyists.

column1: Resume. Your cover letter says you train new team members. Tell us more.
column2:
Process, ethics, mentoring.
Ameren’s Government Relations team works in a decentralized model, so there is no formal supervisor on each issue. When new people join, I train them on how our department works, bill tracking, expert routing and reporting, and on our ethics expectations. I also guide our contract lobbyists on the issues I lead, and I have mentored people outside the department, including a former Senate staffer who went on to a manager role.

column1: Resume. Tell us about the Illinois Utility Business Diversity Council.
column2:
Vice chair, fair and open doors.
I served as Vice Chair from 2016 to 2019. The council brings Illinois utilities together on supplier diversity. As vice chair, I [add one thing you led or the council accomplished]. It reinforced something I believe, that the best way to open doors is a fair, open process every business can use.

column1: Resume. You wrote that Ameren’s territory is about a third of the General Assembly. How do your relationships carry over to ComEd?
column2:
A third downstate, plus Chicago ties, both sides of the aisle.
My relationships run on both sides of the aisle. Legislators from the Ameren Illinois territory make up about a third of the General Assembly, and I have kept them informed on reliability, constituent concerns and storm restoration for years. I have also built relationships with Chicago-area legislators on the many issues that cross both regions. ComEd needs both. City and suburban members, and downstate votes when a bill has to pass statewide.
